question: A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-minute episode of a tonic-clonic seizure. The parents deny any previous history of seizure involving the patient or the family. Physical examination reveals an afebrile, well-groomed, and playful appearance, with normal vital signs. The patient carries a pink birthmark on the right side of her face extending from the forehead to the zygomatic arch. Which of the following findings is most likely on a head CT of this patient?

enhanced_information: The presentation of a 2-year-old girl with a tonic-clonic seizure, no family history of seizures, and a pink birthmark on the face suggests consideration of Sturge-Weber syndrome. This condition is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) and neurological abnormalities, including seizures. The most common neuroimaging finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification, often described as 'tram-track' calcifications on CT. analysis: The clinical presentation of a 2-year-old girl with a tonic-clonic seizure and a facial birthmark suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome. This condition is characterized by a facial port-wine stain and neurological abnormalities, including seizures. The most common neuroimaging finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification, often described as 'tram-track' calcifications on CT. Given the presence of the facial birthmark and the seizure, the most likely finding on a head CT is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification. This aligns with the consensus understanding of Sturge-Weber syndrome's typical presentation and imaging findings.
